headline: A Guest in Orbit, Two-Way Viruses and the Last 50 Animals
teaser: Is a one-week guest astronaut real science or diplomacy? Can evolution run in both directions? And should we spend money saving species down to their last 50 animals?

articles.title: A Guest Aboard Tiangong: Pakistan's First Astronaut Heads to China's Space Station
articles.dek: For the first time, a foreign astronaut is flying to China's space station. Is a one-week guest mission real science, clever diplomacy, or the first step toward a new space nation?

sources.name: Associated Press via ABC News, 24 Nov 2026

paras: At 8:18 on Wednesday morning, Beijing time, a Long March-2F rocket rose from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in the Gobi Desert, carrying the Shenzhou-24 spacecraft and three astronauts. Two of them, commander Tang Hongbo and pilot Wu Yi, are Chinese. The third, Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, is not. The 40-year-old from Pakistan is set to become his country's first astronaut in orbit and the first foreign national ever to board Tiangong, the space station China has operated since late 2022. For a program that has so far flown only its own citizens, the launch marks a symbolic turning point.

Ali's journey began with a cooperation agreement signed in February 2025 between Pakistan's space agency, SUPARCO, and the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA). Under the deal, Pakistani candidates would train in China, and Ali, a former air force pilot, was chosen as one of two candidates before being selected for this flight. The training turned out to be demanding in unexpected ways. Tang, who is now making his third trip to Tiangong, told reporters that every label and manual on board is written in Chinese, and that Ali had begun studying the language with virtually no foundation. Yet at a press conference before the launch, Ali delivered part of his remarks in Mandarin.

Ali's stay will be short. He is expected to spend about a week on the station as a payload specialist before returning to Earth aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft. During that time, he will run four joint China-Pakistan projects in biotechnology and materials science, including an experiment on photosynthetic cyanobacteria, tiny organisms that turn sunlight into chemical energy. His Chinese crewmates have a far longer agenda. According to the CMSA, the mission will carry out more than 90 experiments and technology tests, from organ chips that model how blood vessels age to new kinds of rocket propellant. Meanwhile, Zhu Yangzhu, commander of the previous crew, will remain on Tiangong for about a year to study how the human body copes with long periods in space, a record for a Chinese astronaut.

Supporters see the flight as a sign that space exploration is becoming less exclusive. For decades, the main route into orbit for astronauts from smaller countries was the International Space Station (ISS), run by the United States, Russia and their partners, which is scheduled to be retired around 2030. A second door, they argue, gives developing nations a chance to train scientists, inspire students and take part in research they could never afford alone. Ali himself framed the mission in these terms, insisting that it is "not a finish line" and that what comes after the flight matters more than the flight itself. Speaking to Pakistani children, he urged them to look up at the sky and remember that he is "up there with your dreams."

Not everyone is persuaded that the benefits are as large as the symbolism. Critics of so-called guest missions point out that a single week in orbit produces limited science, and that a visiting astronaut usually performs experiments designed and controlled by the host. In their view, such flights can work as diplomacy as much as research: China gains a showcase for its station and a reliable partner, while the visiting country gains national pride but little lasting capability. A space program, they argue, is built from engineers, factories and long-term budgets, not from a single famous passenger. There is also the question of dependence. A country that reaches orbit only on another nation's rocket remains, in practical terms, a customer.

Both sides have a point. History suggests that early guest flights can matter more than their scientific output. Many of the first astronauts from Asia, Africa and Latin America flew on Soviet or American spacecraft in the 1970s and 1980s, and some of their countries went on to expand their own space programs and satellite industries. Whether Pakistan follows that path will depend less on this week than on the decisions that come after it, such as whether trained scientists are given jobs, funding and research questions at home.

The flight also fits into a wider race. China is preparing to land astronauts on the Moon by 2030, while NASA aims to return Americans to the lunar surface in 2028. Both countries are building coalitions of partners, and offering seats, training and shared experiments is one way to attract them. For students watching the launch, then, the real question may not be who rode the rocket, but who will be designing the next one.

speak.p: Some people think that sending one astronaut to another country's space station is a valuable first step for a developing country. Others think the money should be spent on building local science and engineering skills instead. Which view do you agree with, and why?
speak.hint: Choose one side; give two reasons (inspiration, training, cost, independence); add an example; finish with a one-sentence conclusion.

write.p:
Dr. Lin: This week, Pakistan's first astronaut flew to China's space station for about a week. Some people say short "guest missions" like this are mostly symbolic. Others say they can launch a country's space program. In your opinion, are guest missions a good use of a developing country's resources? Why or why not?
Sara: "Yes. One astronaut can inspire millions of students to study science and engineering. That kind of motivation is hard to buy any other way, and it can shape a whole generation."
Kevin: "I'm not convinced. A week in orbit produces little science, and the country still depends on another nation's rocket. The money would do more good if it were spent on local labs and universities."
steps: State your position clearly in the first sentence.
Respond to Sara or Kevin and add a new reason.
Support it with a fact from the article (one week, four joint projects, the ISS retiring).

articles.title: Tiny Viruses, Big Questions: Evolution on a Two-Way Street
articles.dek: Newly found viruses carry features of both viruses and cell compartments. Did evolution run in both directions, and how far can computer-based discoveries be trusted?
paras: Most people think of viruses as invaders: tiny packages of genetic material that hijack living cells to make copies of themselves. But viruses are also among the oldest and most abundant biological entities on Earth, and their history is tangled up with the history of life itself. A study published in Nature Communications by researchers at the University of Miami now suggests that this tangle is even more complicated than scientists had assumed. Some of the protein structures that viruses use, it appears, may have passed back and forth between viruses and cells more than once.

To understand the finding, it helps to know how a virus protects its genes. Many viruses wrap their DNA in a protein shell called a capsid. A large group of them, including many viruses that infect bacteria, build this shell from proteins that fold into the same three-dimensional shape, known as the HK97 fold. Copies of these proteins lock together like tiles to form a hollow, closed container. Before the shell is filled with DNA and becomes mature, it exists in an earlier form called a procapsid.

Strikingly, the same fold also appears inside ordinary cells. Many bacteria and archaea produce encapsulins, hollow protein compartments that enclose chemical reactions, keeping certain enzymes and their products separate from the rest of the cell. Because encapsulins and viral capsids share such a similar structure, scientists had generally believed that encapsulins evolved from viruses: at some point, a cell borrowed a viral shell and put it to new use. In this view, the flow of evolution ran in one direction only, from virus to cell.

The Miami team, led by doctoral student Abelardo Aguilar and biologist Antoni Luque, did not look for new viruses in the laboratory. Instead, they searched databases containing billions of DNA sequences collected from soil, seawater, wastewater and the human gut, much of it stored in a public database called IMG/M. Using bioinformatics, models of protein physics, protein language models and the structure-prediction program AlphaFold, they identified previously unknown small viruses. "The majority of viruses cannot be grown in the lab," Luque explained, a limitation that makes computer-based searches increasingly valuable.

What the team found were viruses with unusually small and simple genomes that carry features of both viral capsids and encapsulins. Rather than fitting neatly on one side of the line, they seem to sit in between. The researchers argue that this pattern is best explained by bidirectional evolution: viruses gave rise to encapsulins, but encapsulin-like compartments may also have given rise to viruses, and this may have happened repeatedly. They also propose that procapsids could have served as a bridge, supporting both genetic functions, such as holding DNA, and metabolic ones, such as hosting chemical reactions. "One implication of this research is the possibility that viral capsids could also facilitate biochemical reactions," Aguilar said.

Not every scientist will accept this conclusion without more evidence. The viruses were identified from genetic sequences and computer models rather than isolated and observed directly, so their actual structures and behavior remain predictions. Even the university's own summary describes them as possible evolutionary intermediates and notes that further research is needed to establish the proposed functions. Skeptics could also point out that similar shapes do not always prove a simple story of shared ancestry: when two structures look alike, it can be difficult to tell which came first, or whether both descend from an older ancestor that has since disappeared.

Even so, the study shows how quickly biology is changing. Tools originally designed to predict protein shapes are now being used to explore parts of nature that no one can grow in a dish, and Luque has said the same approach can be applied in other contexts. If the bidirectional model holds up, it would blur the familiar boundary between viruses and the cells they infect, and it might encourage engineers to think of viral shells as tiny reaction chambers rather than mere packaging. For now, the safest conclusion is a modest one: evolution does not always travel in one direction, and some of its most important routes may run both ways.

articles.title: Down to the Last 50: Can Species Come Back from the Brink?
articles.dek: A study of 141 nearly lost species finds that recovery is possible but rarely happens without help. Should limited money go to the rarest animals or to those most likely to survive?

sources.name: Proceedings of the Royal Society B (DOI 10.1098/rspb.2026.2436)

paras: When a species falls to its last few dozen animals, conservationists face an uncomfortable question: is it still worth saving, or has the battle already been lost? A new study published in Proceedings of the Royal Society B offers one of the clearest answers yet. Researchers led by Donal Smith of Monash University in Australia examined 141 bird and mammal species whose wild populations had dropped below 50 individuals at some point since 1950. Their conclusion is both hopeful and sobering: species on the brink can recover, but they rarely do so on their own.

The contrast in the data is stark. Of the 51 species that received direct conservation help, such as captive breeding, the removal of predators or the movement of animals to safer sites, 31 (61%) climbed back to at least 100 individuals, while six went extinct. Of the 90 species that received no direct intervention, only two (2%) reached 100 animals, and 33 (37%) disappeared entirely. Recovery also took patience. Among the species that were helped and recovered, the median time needed to reach 100 animals was 18 years, longer than many political careers and most funding cycles.

The study also suggests that some kinds of help work better than others. Recovery was most common when conservationists tackled the original cause of decline, such as introduced predators or habitat loss, while also using hands-on methods like captive breeding or translocation, which means moving animals to a new, safer location. By contrast, legal protection and other indirect measures on their own showed no clear link with recovery. In other words, a law that forbids hunting a bird may be necessary, but it is unlikely to be sufficient if rats are still eating its eggs.

The Lord Howe woodhen, a flightless bird found only on a small island off eastern Australia, illustrates the point. By the late 1970s, just 23 birds remained. Conservationists removed feral pigs and cats and bred birds in captivity, and the population stabilized at around 200 for decades. That was enough to avoid extinction, but not enough to make the species secure. The real breakthrough came only after rats were eradicated from the island in 2019; by 2024, the population had risen to 1,638.

Such successes were not always expected. In 1974, the Mauritius kestrel, a small bird of prey from the Indian Ocean, was reduced to just four wild birds, and in 1979 the environmental scientist Norman Myers suggested that conservation money might be better spent on species with better prospects. This idea, often called conservation triage, borrows its logic from emergency medicine: when resources are limited, help those most likely to survive. The kestrel's story complicates that logic. After captive breeding, predator control and releases, its numbers climbed into the hundreds, although they have since declined again.

The authors are careful not to overstate their findings. Because the study compares outcomes rather than running a controlled experiment, it cannot prove that intervention caused recovery. Species whose problems were easier to solve may simply have been more likely to receive help in the first place. Reaching 100 animals is also not the same as being safe: many recovered species still depend on intensive, expensive management, and a single new disease or invasive predator could undo decades of work.

The research does not settle the triage debate, but it shifts the burden of proof. Critics of costly rescue programs can still argue that money spent on a handful of rare birds might protect far more habitat, and far more species, elsewhere. Supporters reply that the two goals are not always in conflict, since removing rats or cats from an island helps many animals at once. What the numbers do show is that the alternative to intervention is usually not a slow recovery but extinction. For a species down to its last 50, doing nothing is itself a decision, and the study suggests it is usually a fatal one.

parts.title: Multiple-choice cloze
parts.task: Read the text and decide which answer (A, B, C or D) best fits each gap.
parts.text: When Shenzhou-24 lifted off this week, it carried the first foreign astronaut ever to board China's space station. For Pakistan, the flight is a source of great national {1}. Its astronaut had to {2} a great deal of effort into learning Chinese, since every manual on board is written in that language. Supporters say the mission will {3} rise to a new generation of young scientists. Critics, {4} the other hand, argue that a single week in orbit can hardly {5} a difference to a country's scientific capability. They also point out that guest astronauts usually carry out experiments that have been designed by their hosts. Whether the flight proves to be a turning point will {6} largely on what happens after it. If Pakistan uses the moment to {7} up its investment in research, the mission could {8} the foundations for a lasting space program.

items.why: "A source of national pride" is a fixed collocation. "Proud" is an adjective, and "honor" and "glory" do not collocate naturally with "a source of great national" here.
We "put effort into" something. "Make an effort" exists, but it is not followed by "into"; "do" and "take" do not combine with "effort into".
"Give rise to" means to cause something to develop. "Bring", "make" and "take" do not combine with "rise to" in this meaning.
"On the other hand" introduces a contrasting view. The other prepositions do not form this phrase.
"Make a difference" means to have an important effect. We do not say "do/give/bring a difference".
"Depend on" means to be decided by. "Rely on" and "count on" mean to trust someone, and "base" needs a passive or object (be based on).
"Step up" means to increase the amount or speed of something, as in "step up investment". "Set up", "pick up" and "make up" do not mean increase.
"Lay the foundations for" is the fixed collocation meaning to create the basis for something.

parts.title: Open cloze
parts.task: Read the text and think of the word which best fits each gap. Use only one word in each gap.
parts.text: Viruses are usually thought {9} as invaders that take over living cells. Yet a new study suggests that their history is far more complicated {10} scientists had assumed. Researchers at the University of Miami did not grow viruses in a laboratory; instead, they searched huge databases {11} contained billions of DNA sequences. {12} the help of AI tools, they identified small viruses with features of both viral shells and cell compartments. {13} only do these viruses challenge the old idea that evolution ran in one direction, but they also hint that viral shells might host chemical reactions. Even so, the results need to be treated with caution, {14} the viruses have not yet been observed directly. Until they are, their structures will remain predictions rather {15} facts. As one researcher put {16}, most viruses simply cannot be grown in the lab.

items.why: "Think of something as something" means to regard it in a particular way; in the passive: "are thought of as".
"More complicated than" completes a comparative structure.
A relative pronoun introduces a defining clause about "databases"; both "that" and "which" are possible.
"With the help of" means using or assisted by something.
"Not only do ... but (they) also ..." is an inverted structure used for emphasis.
A reason connector is needed: "as", "since" or "because" all explain why caution is needed.
"Rather than" means instead of.
"As someone put it" introduces a reported way of saying something.

parts.title: Word formation
parts.task: Use the word given in capitals to form a word that fits in the gap.
parts.text: When a species falls to its last 50 animals, its {17} is far from guaranteed. A new study of 141 birds and mammals shows that most species recover only after direct {18} by conservationists. Without help, more than a third of them went {19}. The most effective projects tackled the original causes of decline, such as {20} predators, while also breeding animals in captivity. Legal protection on its own, by contrast, proved surprisingly {21}. The authors admit that their findings are not {22}, because they could not run a controlled experiment. Nevertheless, the results make it {23} clear that doing nothing is rarely a safe choice. For conservationists facing {24} budgets, that is an important message.

items.why: A noun is needed after the possessive "its": survive → survival.
After the adjective "direct" we need a noun: intervene → intervention.
"Go extinct" needs an adjective: extinction → extinct.
An adjective describes "predators": invade → invasive.
The sense is negative ("by contrast", "on its own"), so add the prefix: effect → effective → ineffective.
Findings that cannot prove cause are "not conclusive": conclude → conclusive.
An adverb modifies "clear"; "abundantly clear" is a common collocation.
"Limited budgets" uses the past participle as an adjective.

parts.title: Key word transformation
parts.task: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first sentence, using the word given. Do not change the word given. Use between three and six words, including the word given.

items.why: Passive reporting structure: "were thought to have + past participle" refers to an earlier action.

items.s1: The woodhen's numbers only rose sharply after rats were removed.
items.why: "Only after" = "not ... until": the rise did not happen until rats were removed.

items.s1: If conservationists had not helped, the kestrel would probably have died out.
items.post: , the kestrel would probably have died out.
items.why: "But for + noun" = "if it had not been for", replacing an "if ... not" clause.
